summary: Granite tower (1847) on a ledge off Maine, first lit in 1830; the 1902 wreck of the tug Astral; automated in 1977; now a College of the Atlantic research station, not open to the public.

access.note: Owned by the College of the Atlantic; not open to the public (US Lighthouse Society). Best viewed by boat (New England Lighthouses).

events.note: Congress allocates $5,000 for a lighthouse on the rock (LighthouseFriends)
Station established; stone dwelling with wooden tower (USLHS; LighthouseFriends)
Original light completed in summer 1830 by Joseph Berry (LighthouseFriends)
Present granite tower built with a $15,000 authorization (USLHS; LighthouseFriends)
Mariners ask for a fog bell (LighthouseFriends)
New lantern room supplied by the Lighthouse Board (LighthouseFriends gives 1857)
Original third-order Fresnel lens (USLHS). LighthouseFriends dates the lens to 1857; see resolved_conflicts
One-and-a-half-story frame dwelling built south of the stone house (LighthouseFriends)
Leaking stone parapet removed; cast-iron lantern deck and gallery installed (LighthouseFriends)
Forty-five-foot bell tower erected (LighthouseFriends)
Third-class Daboll trumpet in operation November 30, 1891 (Light-House Board report; LighthouseFriends)
Prefabricated wooden duplex replaces the stone dwelling, linked to the tower by a walkway (LighthouseFriends; Light-House Board report)
Revolving fourth-order Fresnel lens; characteristic changed to a white flash every fifteen seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Tug Astral wrecked on the northeast ledge, December 9, 1902. The accounts differ on the rescue; see wrecks
Keepers rescue Lafayette Carter, October 1912 (LighthouseFriends)
Assistant keeper Henry C. Ray drowns during an attempted landing (LighthouseFriends; not confirmed in a newspaper)
First assistant Arthur E. Ginn tows a disabled powerboat to the station (LighthouseFriends)
Radiobeacon installed; its power plant electrifies the station (Lighthouse Service Bulletin; LighthouseFriends)
Last two keepers taken off by helicopter just before Christmas 1977 (USLHS; LighthouseFriends)
Transferred to the College of the Atlantic under the Maine Lights Program (LighthouseFriends)
Hurricane Bill damages several station buildings and nearly destroys the boathouse; the lighthouse is not damaged (LighthouseFriends)
Listed on the National Register (LighthouseFriends says it is listed; year from the record, not checked in a source read)

corrections.why: The standing granite tower is the 1847 tower (USLHS: tower established 1847). The 1830 light was a stone dwelling with a wooden tower (LighthouseFriends).
USLHS lists the owner and manager as the College of the Atlantic; LighthouseFriends says the station was transferred to the college in 1998 under the Maine Lights Program.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1830 (USLHS, Rowlett) and 1847 (Wikidata, OSM). The sources agree that the station was first lit in 1830 with a stone dwelling and wooden tower, and that the granite tower now standing dates from 1847. The record's 1830 tower date is the first light station, not the present tower.
LighthouseFriends dates the third-order Fresnel lens to 1857; the USLHS record gives 1858.

LighthouseFriends says the keepers rescued seventeen men and one froze to death. The Rockland dispatch in the Worcester Spy says Capt. Sorensen of the tug Clara Clarita rescued a party of sixteen men, and that the mess boy was washed into the sea. The story gives both and does not choose.
The roster lists Ray as first assistant 1918-1920 and as head keeper for 1920. LighthouseFriends calls him an assistant keeper when he drowned.
LighthouseFriends gives twenty-six miles from the nearest harbor. Lewis (1842, quoted by LighthouseFriends) gives twelve miles from the nearest land. The measures differ.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: USLHS place record and roster (185 lines, matched by name and position at 0.93 km; contractor names and USCG lines kept as the roster prints them); LighthouseFriends (copyrighted: paraphrased; Lewis, Derby and Ward quotations are taken from LighthouseFriends's quotations of 19th-century reports, and the originals were not read); Light-House Board reports FY1892 (scan pages 340, 374) and FY1893 (scan page 53), from the corpus, with printed page numbers not confirmed; Lighthouse Service Bulletins 1932 p. 8 and 1934 p. 21 (the 1934 article reprints the Sunday American Weekly of 12 August 1934); Worcester Spy 16 December 1902 p. 8 (a Rockland dispatch of 15 December; the Portland Daily Press of 15 December was not read); New England Lighthouses (used for accessibility only). The NRHP nomination (88000155) is listed on the NPS placeholder: 'not yet digitized', so it is not cited; the 1988 listing year comes from the record and is not confirmed in a source read. Newspaper search for the 1920 drowning returned no hit, so that death rests on LighthouseFriends alone. Left out on purpose: keepers' family and medical details in LighthouseFriends, and the name of a 1977 Coast Guard keeper (a living person; the roster does not name him). The Mars family's 2014 gift is named as published by LighthouseFriends. Distance and lens date conflicts are noted in resolved_conflicts. The New England Lighthouses page gives the keeper's house as 1893; USLHS and LighthouseFriends give 1892 for the duplex; not resolved here. The Wikipedia lead gives an 18 nautical mile distance and a 1858 lens; not cited. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27 (independent pass): The Bulletin of 1934 (PDF p. 21, title 'Transport Garden 2½ Miles to Sea') gives 2½ miles from the mainland, a third distance beside LighthouseFriends' 26 miles from the nearest harbor and Lewis's 12 miles from the nearest land; the story now states all three. The story no longer says the first light was lit in 1830 (USLHS and LighthouseFriends give the station's establishment and the completion, not a lighting date). Roster counts (43 principal keepers, 42 first assistants, 49 second assistants, 51 other names: 3 contractors, 1 superintendent of construction, 47 USCG lines) are my tally of the USLHS roster lines; the story says 'Coast Guard personnel' because the roster prints the heading 'USCG', not 'officers'. Arthur E. Ginn: LighthouseFriends calls him 'First Assistant' in its 1923 rescue, but its own keepers list and the USLHS roster list him as head keeper from 1923; the story gives no title, for the editor to resolve. Carter's 'nothing to eat for six days' is Carter's own letter, quoted by LighthouseFriends; the story says so. Astral: LighthouseFriends (keepers rescue 17, one frozen) and the Worcester Spy of 16 December 1902 (Captain Sorensen rescues 16 from the rock; the mess boy Frank Cummings washed into the sea) disagree on the rescuer, the number saved and the death; the story states this and does not choose. Living people: the keepers named (1920-1936) ended their connection with the station before about 1960; the 2014 Mars gift is named as LighthouseFriends prints it. The 1977 Coast Guard keeper named on LighthouseFriends (Douglas Nute) is not named in the story. Printed page numbers of the Light-House Board volumes (FY1892 scan pp. 340 and 374; FY1893 scan p. 53) were not confirmed from the page images; the corpus gives printed pages only with '?'. The 1934 Bulletin article's OCR reads '2:l miles' for '2½ miles'; the evidence quote keeps the OCR text. Wording: the Coast Guard supply sentence and the 1932 radiobeacon sentence were reworded (the radiobeacon source is the 1932 Bulletin itself, which states the candlepower change). The NRHP nomination (88000155) remains unavailable and is not cited.
